entries.title: African Parks: When conservation becomes a question of power
entries.summary: African Parks is dedicated to protecting wildlife on the continent across some vast areas. But the organization faces allegations of human rights abuses by rangers. Now, Prince Harry is stepping down from its board.
entries.content:
September 10, 2026

African Parks is dedicated to protecting wildlife on the continent across some vast areas. But the organization faces allegations of human rights abuses by rangers. Now, Prince Harry is stepping down from its board.

Prince Harry has long been a supporter of African wildlife and nature. When the British royal first became involved with African Parks in 2016, he served as a prominent figure supporting awareness on elephant conservation.

Later, the son of King Charles III became president of the organization before joining its board in 2023.

But reports indicate that in just a few weeks' time, he will step down from his position at African Parks. The NGO claims that the move is merely part of a reshuffling of its board.

But Dutch journalist and author Olivier van Beemen, who has extensively investigated the South Africa-based wildlife conservation group, believes the association between Harry and African Parks has increasingly become a burden — for both sides.

Prince harming

Harry's role was to mainly open doors for African Parks, van Beemen says. His fame attracted media attention and helped the NGO gain access to potential donors. But his notorious falling-out with his family increasingly failed to improve the organization's coffers and image.

At the same time, allegations of human rights abuses at African Parks made the prince's association with the organization increasingly problematic.

"I think they now see each other more as a liability," van Beemen told DW, stressing that the full story reaches far beyond a junior member of the royal family simply stepping down from a ribbon-cutting role.

An NGO with state-like powers

According to its own figures, African Parks manages 24 protected areas in 13 African countries, covering more than 20 million hectares. By 2030, the organization aims to manage as many as 30 parks.

Its business model is known as delegated management: African governments hand over the long-term management of protected areas to the group.

The land formally remains state-owned. But the organization takes on wide-ranging responsibilities, including conservation, infrastructure, tourism and anti-poaching operations.

For African governments, this model offers a major advantage: African Parks brings international funding, expertise and personnel to protected areas that many states would otherwise struggle to manage on their own.

In order to achieve its objectives on the ground, African Parks employs a host of armed rangers across the continent, who are allowed to use indelicate methods if and when needed; in some cases, its influence even extends to managing border controls.

"They take over the state's monopoly on the use of force within the park," says van Beemen, adding that some critics of the NGO have gone as far as describing African Parks as a "state within a state."

It is in this context that mounting allegations of human rights abuses have been recorded in recent years, with conservation efforts repeatedly coming into conflict with local communities.

The shadow of the Baka case

The worst allegations of rights abuses relate to Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo, which emerged in 2023.

Members of the indigenous Baka community reported violence, torture and sexual abuse at the hands of African Parks' rangers.

The NGO subsequently commissioned the London-based firm Omnia Strategy to investigate the allegations, resulting in African Parks acknowledging certain instances of human rights abuses two years later — though the full investigation report was never made public.

According to van Beemen, the report was not even shown to the government of the Republic of Congo, despite African Parks operating there under an agreement with the government. To this day, it remains unclear what exactly happened in Odzala-Kokoua, and how many people were affected.

African Parks has promised reforms, merely highlighting alleged failures in its own systems and processes in the past but has remained intransparent about the entire scandal, says van Beemen.

Division over findings in Dutch book

The Dutch journalist has meanwhile published a book on the whole affair, titled "Beasts and Men." The volume won several awards in the Netherlands, and has attracted international attention.

But African Parks fundamentally rejects van Beemen's portrayal of the organization, saying his book contains "hundreds of factual inaccuracies" as well as "a similar number of deeply misleading statements."

Regarding the human rights allegations, African Parks says some of the cases described by van Beemen had occurred outside the NGOs control.

At the same time, it stressed in a statement that it has a zero-tolerance policy toward abuse, and that there is training in place on human rights training as well as a detailed complaints mechanisms.

But as part of his research, van Beemen also spoke to several former rangers and people affected by conservation operations in several African countries, where he says he repeatedly encountered a fundamental problem perpetuated by African Parks: the loose definition of what constitutes poaching.

According to the accounts he collected, the NGO also treats some locals who hunt animals for their own consumption as poachers, rather than using the terms exclusive to describe professional poachers who kill rhinos or elephants for international criminal networks.

Van Beemen said that during his research in Zambia, former rangers told him about the brutal treatment the people taken into custody on such grounds can face: "This can involve beatings. It can involve very serious torture," he told DW.

Hiding behind a colonial mindset?

The history of African Parks is also controversial. The organization was founded by Dutch businessman Paul Fentener van Vlissingen, who — according to van Beemen — refused to accept the international economic sanctions against the South African apartheid system during the 1980s.

A former close associate of the founde told the Dutch journalist that at the top echolons of the organization, Africans were allegedly considered incapable of protecting their own natural resources because they lacked the money and management skills to do so.

In its early years, African Parks was headquartered in the Netherlands where according to van Beemen, employees would routinely look at maps of Africa and plan where the organization could take over additional parks.

"For me, it was very difficult not to think of the colonialists of earlier centuries looking at the same maps and searching for opportunities for colonial expansion," van Beemen told Dw.

African Parks meanwhile also rejects this characterization, pointing out at the relevant contracts it has signed with African governments.

Conservation and accountability

The scandal also hits closer to Europe not only because of Prince Harry's departure from the NGO but also due to the fact that European and German funding also goes to projects involving African Parks.

The organization stresses that cooperations with local communities is at the heart of its work:

It says that there are people living in 64% of the areas it manages, while legal access to resources is allowed in 90% of the parks. Only four of the 23 parks are fully fenced, it added.

But without sufficient scrutiny and accountability, there is no way of verifying the details behind those claims, as the image of the NGO continues to tank.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: North Korea spends war windfall on arms, infrastructure
entries.summary: The Ukraine war and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have delivered an economic boost to North Korea, allowing the regime to pursue a range of long-desired projects.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea spends war windfall on arms, infrastructure

September 10, 2026

The Ukraine war and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have delivered an economic boost to North Korea, allowing the regime to pursue a range of long-desired projects.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is spending the money that his troops have earned fighting in Ukraine to fund a long wish list of projects that were previously beyond his financial reach.

South Korea's National Intelligence Service estimated in May that Pyongyang received a minimum of $7.7 billion (€6.6 billion) in financial aid and economic value from Russia in the preceding three years for committing men and materiel to Moscow's war against Ukraine — and potentially as much as $14 billion.

That is a significant amount given that the North's GDP for 2024 stood at $26.6 billion.

Kim's support for Russia has been lucrative, and a slew of reports are now identifying where that money is being spent.

A portion of the funds is being put aside for the Regional Development 20x10 Policy, unveiled in January 2024 and which aims to construct modern industrial facilities in 20 regional cities per year for the next 10 years to improve living standards outside Pyongyang.

Benefiting from Russian money

More civil programs are being designed, observers say, although most appear to be earmarked for the "elites" who reside in Pyongyang.

"Before the alliance with Russia, the general infrastructure was poor due to a mixture of economic mismanagement and sanctions," said Martyn Williams, senior fellow for the Korea program at the Stimson Center in Washington DC.

"With the breakdown in consensus on the United Nations Security Council and renewed trade with China and Russia, things are starting to move along now," he told DW.

"There are several large programs to build factories and hospitals across the country, [Kim] has ordered the development of entire new districts of Pyongyang and there's a rural housing project building tens of thousands of rural homes," he said, along with investment in "the modernization of several sectors of the economy."

There are, however, structural problems that still need to be overcome, he said.

"There is investment going into building, but the large new hospital in central Pyongyang was built some time ago and sat unused for a while, until medicines and equipment could be procured," he said. "North Korea is great at building, but keeping it running is the key — so we look to see if that will happen."

IAEA warns of new nuclear facility

More of the financial windfall is clearly being put into the military. On Wednesday, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it had identified a new uranium enrichment facility at the Yongbyon Nuclear Complex with an estimated 28 cascades of centrifuges.

The IAEA estimated that the facility would permit the regime to produce 85 kilograms of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year, enough for four nuclear warheads.

Satellite images also show that the North is enlarging and upgrading the west coast port of Nampo and Chongjin, on the east coast of the peninsula, to accommodate a new generation of warships.

On Monday, Kim attended the commissioning ceremony in Wonsan of the 5,000-ton destroyer Kang Kon, with the North Korean leader claiming the vessel was capable of launching nuclear weapons and would be able to "deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies."

The third area of heavy investment has been in major improvements in roads, ports and bridges. This is infrastructure that stagnated during years of isolation under international sanctions but is today required to facilitate the deployment of more troops to Russia and the arrival of advanced military technology, energy and consumer goods in return.

On Tuesday, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, with customs posts and warehousing facilities under construction on both sides of the waterway. The bridge underlines the rapidly expanding ties since Kim and President Vladimir Putin announced a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024.

The route will permit greater truck-borne exchanges, reduce costs and potentially be used for the transit of North Korean men, weapons and ammunition to Russia. It also further reduces the leverage of sanctions on North Korea.

"A lot of these projects, such as improving trans-border rail and road connections, building customs facilities and so on, were started before the pandemic and have followed an on-again-off-again pattern ever since," said Marcus Noland, executive vice president at the Peterson Institute for International Economics in Washington.

"After difficult times during the pandemic, which was accompanied by border closure, the North Korean economy appears to have grown for the last several years on the back of Ukraine war revenues and cybercrime."

Hinterland 'stagnating'

Noland said he has the impression that Pyongyang is faring relatively well economically, along with a number of cities on the China border thanks to renewed trade, "but the hinterland continues to stagnate."

While the Ukraine conflict and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have been an economic boon to North Korea, analysts say, it's not clear what will happen when the war inevitably comes to an end.

"The North Korean regime could be in a difficult spot if peace were to break out in Ukraine," said Noland. "If the war-related revenues were to dry up, the country could experience an economic decline and associated discontent after a period of rising expectations," he stressed.

"I am not saying that it would be enough to destabilize the system, but I do think that a transition to peace in Ukraine could present challenges that would have to be navigated by the regime."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
entries.summary: The German government wants to follow other EU countries and take more decisive action against Russia's shadow fleet, accusing it of helping Moscow evade sanctions and carry out acts of sabotage.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet

September 10, 2026

The German government wants to follow other EU countries and take more decisive action against Russia's shadow fleet, accusing it of helping Moscow evade sanctions and carry out acts of sabotage.

On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions.

But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage, and possibly drone operations and related disruptions."

Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party. In a recent interview with DW, she complained: "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table," she argued.

She accuses the German government of failing to take action: "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong."

Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet

By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel.

Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior."

In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety, or violate environmental regulations.

Russia's threats: Just a bluff?

It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint is aimed at avoiding an escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the small state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war."

Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded: "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened. Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely steered clear of confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels."

After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said: "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through."

Armed Russian crews on board

Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk: "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board. Those are risks that must be factored into the equation."

Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way.

"It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel."

Inspections would raise costs for Russia

While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone. Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it."

He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy."

This article has been translated from German.

What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

entries.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations
entries.summary: As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers while keeping her loyal older fans.
entries.content:
September 10, 2026

As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers while keeping her loyal older fans.

On September 12, Celine Dion kicks off a series of 26 sold-out concerts, part of a Paris residency held through May 2027. Some 500,000 people are expected to attend the performances, marking the global star's highly anticipated return to the stage following a prolonged break. 

In 2022, she announced that she was battling a rare and incurable neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome. The health issues led her to cancel her world tour.  

In the summer of 2024, she returned to the spotlight atop the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics, her resilience giving hope to fans worldwide.  

Now, in the days ahead of her Paris concerts, Dion has been thrilling hundreds of fans gathered in front of her hotel, taking the time to chat with them for a few minutes every day, sometimes even joining them in spontaneous sing-alongs and dances.

The best-selling Canadian artist of all time, Dion has released a total of 27 studio albums, sold more than 200 million records worldwide and earned multiple Grammy Awards. 

Even though her most defining hits date back to the 1990s, she is more than a nostalgia act, as her appeal is now skyrocketing with Gen Z and millennial listeners.

How did that happen?

A modern fashion darling

In her daily exchanges with her fans on her way to rehearsal, she's always wearing fresh couture pieces: an asymmetrical Loewe gown, a bold blue Givenchy leather dress by Sarah Burton or a striking jacket by Tom Ford.

"Celine Dion is turning the streets of Paris into her runway," wrote Vogue magazine in reaction to her stylish outfits.

"She's always really been into fashion, already in the 1990s, even though we long didn't know this," says Quebec cultural reporter Stephane Leclair, author and host of a podcast series on the star's "D'eux" album. "You know, Celine Dion was never considered 'cool.' She's always had that slightly corny, slightly goofy side. But through her genuine interest for fashion, she’s managed to revamp her image quite a bit."

A notable move came in 2016: Dion admired Zendaya's edgy red carpet looks so much that she tracked down her stylist, Law Roach, and asked him to team up with her. She credits Roach with transforming her into a modern fashion darling.

But that's just one aspect that explains her ongoing — and renewed — popularity.

A rags to riches story

Born on March 30, 1968, Celine Dion was the youngest of 14 children of a poor family in French-speaking in Quebec, Canada. As she proudly notes on her official website, the house was so full that, as a baby, she had to sleep in a drawer instead of a crib. 

She grew up surrounded by music, and recorded her first song at the age of 12. It impressed music manager Rene Angelil so much that he mortgaged his house to pay for her first record. She quickly emerged as a child star in Quebec.

Inspired by Michael Jackson, she decided that she wanted to become a megastar. She won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988 and launched her first English-language album, "Unison," in 1990.

This, however, sparked cultural tension among French-speaking fans in Quebec, who felt she was neglecting her roots to pursue American and international superstardom.

"We were between two referendums on Quebec's independence at the time," points out Leclair.

But even after she became a global star, Dion proudly kept identifying as the "little girl from Charlemagne," the small town near Montreal where she grew up.

"People in Quebec quickly understood that it didn't change anything, that she would always remain one of them, and that it only added another layer to her career," notes Leclair.

Indeed, she also kept working in French all while building her career as a global pop artist. Teaming up with popular French song-writer Jean-Jacques Goldman, they released "D'eux" in 1995. It became the best-selling French-language album of all time.

The theme song for "Beauty and the Beast" (1991) won her both a Grammy and an Academy Award, while her best-selling "My Heart Will Go On" (1997) for the blockbuster film "Titanic" cemented her status alongside music's greatest vocalists. 

Adding groundbreaking edge to Las Vegas

While other aging stars would head to the Las Vegas Strip to finish their careers, Dion revolutionized the music industry with "A New Day...," her high-profile residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace: With a total of 714 performances from 2003 to 2007, she demonstrated how such residencies could be modern, cutting-edge — and extremely lucrative.

It served as a blueprint for Las Vegas residencies by younger stars, such as Britney Spears and Adele. 

Viral authenticity

"The world's biggest stars are often dead set on protecting a perfect, untouchable image. Celine, on the other hand, is incredibly accessible. She isn't afraid to let her true, authentic personality shine through," points out Leclair.

"And Celine's die-hard fans just love her humorous side," he adds. "They love the fact that she's a bit wacky. It makes her really relatable."

Famous for spontaneously breaking into song during interviews, those moments, as well as various over-the-top scenes from her 1990s music videos, have been picked up in Internet memes and TikTok trends.

Encouraged by her teenage sons, she launched her own official TikTok account in January 2026. She went viral with a "What's in My Bag?" video where she pulls out a mix of everyday essentials and completely unhinged items.

Writing a new chapter

But beyond the humor, she's also ready to share her most vulnerable moments.

In 2016, she lost her husband — her manager, Rene Angelil — and a brother to cancer within the same week. Her 2019 album "Courage" focused on loss and recovery.

Her 2024 documentary "I am: Celine Dion," in which she looks back on her life and career all while addressing how she deals with her stiff-person syndrome diagnosis, has been praised by critics as intensely sincere and visceral.

One scene of the film follows her as she suffers from a painful spasm.

"I don't think many stars of that caliber would have agreed to be filmed — and have the footage included in the final cut — in such an unflattering state," notes Leclair. "It was partly out of a desire for transparency, to explain to her fans why she had to step back."

And her fans highly value this authenticity, as well as her resilience.

She is now undergoing physical and therapies to manage her symptoms and be able to perform again for this series of more than 2-hour-long concerts. They will feature 18 musicians and four backing singers; a live choir will also join them on stage for several songs.

Additionally, Paris will mark the start of the concert series with two giant karaoke sessions on September 11. A total of 10,000 people are expected to take part in the participatory event celebrating her four decades of songs.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

entries.title: Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis
entries.summary: A royal succession committee and the family of late King Oyo Nyimba of Toroo have put forward competing candidates. Questions have been raised as to whether the late monarch indeed had a son as his family claims.
entries.content:
Uganda

Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis

September 10, 2026

A royal succession committee and the family of late King Oyo Nyimba of Toroo have put forward competing candidates. Questions have been raised as to whether the late monarch indeed had a son as his family claims.

Uganda's traditional kingdom of Tooro has been plunged into a sucession crisis after the family of late monarch Oyo Nyimba rejected on Thursday other clan members' choice of successor.

Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence.

Oyo, who was also known by his regnal name Rukidi IV, became the world's youngest monarch at the age of three in 1995 following the death of his father. His ascension celebrations were attended by longtime Ugandan strongman President Yoweri Museveni.

His reign was overseen by a series of relatives acting as regents until he turned 18 in 2010.

He died on August 27 at the age of 34 while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.

Who are the main players in the succession fight?

On Wednesday, the royal clan's succession committee named the late king's cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the next monarch.

Kijanangoma is a television anchor at public broadcaster UBC.

However, Oyo's mother and sister announced on Thursday that they rejected this proposal, indicating that the king had left a will declaring his son his successor.

His mother Queen Kemigisa called the committee a "self-appointed group of clan members" who had named a new king despite knowing the contents of Oyo's will.

She also accused the Ugandan military of placing her family under house arrest.

The identity of Oyo's son and the son's mother remains a mystery. A campaigner for HIV/AIDS prevention and environmental causes, he had not publicly acknowledged a son until Toroo's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced the boy's existence after Oyo's death.

The controversy grew after Andrew Mwenda, a well-known journalist and relative of Oyo's, wrote on social media site X that a son could only succeed a father in Toroo if he was born to a queen, and said that the family had not produced so much as a picture of the boy.

Prime Minister Armstrong called for both sides to remain calm on Thursday, saying the process "should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial."

Oyo's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump
entries.summary: The European Central Bank raised borrowing costs and warned that inflation could remain high for an extended period. Energy markets and geopolitical tensions are still major concerns.
entries.content:
September 10, 2026

The European Central Bank raised borrowing costs and warned that inflation could remain high for an extended period. Energy markets and geopolitical tensions are still major concerns.

The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates on Thursday, hoping to curb rising inflation driven by higher energy costs stemming from the war between the US and Iran. This is the second increase that the ECB has had to implement this year. Rising oil and natural gas prices pushed inflation above 3% in the 21-country eurozone, surpassing the previous target of 2%.

"The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside of inflation and to the downside of economic growth," the ECB said in a statement after its annual meeting, held this year in Berlin.

The ECB also announced its economic growth projection for 2026. The study reveals slight growth of 0.9% compared to 0.8% in June, and inflation is now expected to average 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027.

Without a clear resolution to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which began in late February, energy costs continue to rise, suggesting persistent inflation. There is also growing concern about gas storage levels, which remain below historical norms as the winter heating season approaches.

Economic outlook remains uncertain

"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," according to the ECB.

For countries in the eurozone, another hike in rates means more expensive mortgages, consumer credit, and loans. There has been little indication that eurozone inflation is being passed more broadly through the economy via higher prices for food, goods, or services.

Experts say the European Central Bank is worried about raising rates too slowly again. The last time it needed to take measures at this pace was in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"The inflation outlook has worsened over the summer," said Sylvain Broyer, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa at S&P. "Supply shocks are not only multiplying, but it is increasingly likely that demand is also contributing to inflation," he said.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Are electric vehicles really bad for the environment?
entries.summary: Some German politicians are calling for a delay to the EU plan to phase out gas-powered vehicles, saying cars must be judged on the entire carbon footprint. But the full picture still says EVs are more climate friendly.
entries.content:
September 10, 2026

Some German politicians are calling for a delay to the EU plan to phase out gas-powered vehicles, saying cars must be judged on the entire carbon footprint. But the full picture still says EVs are more climate friendly.

"The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral.

Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand  Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Stepping away from the phaseout, he said, would now be backed by "science."

Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral."

The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix.

Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling.

It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM.

No new insights in TUM report

Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known.

Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%.

Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles.

Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe.

Batteries have a high environmental cost

Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water.

Bieker's ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine.

"We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture.

Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans.

Renewable energy making the case for EVs

The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas.

But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs.

"Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonized and expected to be almost fully decarbonized by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will only strengthen the case even more."

Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules.

"Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of [internal combustion engine] vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed."

Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth

Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy.

"The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia.

EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% of respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns.

"We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: India news: Government proposes elected body for Ladakh
entries.summary: The government has suggested creating an elected Union Territory body. However, Ladakh leaders have expressed disappointment over the slow pace of progress. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Government proposes elected body for Ladakh

Published September 10, 2026last updated September 10, 2026

The government has suggested creating an elected Union Territory body. However, Ladakh leaders have expressed disappointment over the slow pace of progress. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines that are getting India talking on Thursday, September 10:

  • New Dehli taking steps towards creating an elected body for the Kashmir territory of Ladakh
  • Delhi has deployed thousands of security personnel ahead of BRICS Summit this weekend

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Xi Jinping to attend BRICS Summit in India

Xi Jinping to attend BRICS Summit in India

China's President Xi Jinping will visit India over the weekend to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi, the Chinese Foreign Ministry confirmed Thursday.

"At the invitation of Prime Minister of the Republic of India Narendra Modi, President Xi Jinping will attend the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13," the ministry said in a post on X.

This will be Xi's first visit to India in seven years since he attended an informal 2019 summit with Modi in Mamallapuram near Chennai.

Xi's visit holds significance as the diplomatic engagement will have implications for the ongoing efforts to stabilize ties between India and China as well as for BRICS cooperation.

Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit.

Skip next section More than 4 million affected by floods in Bihar

More than 4 million affected by floods in Bihar

Several districts in the eastern state of Bihar have been hit by floods with several rivers flowing above the danger mark at multiple places, officials said on Wednesday.

More than 4 million people across 14 districts of Bihar have been affected by floods that were triggered by incessant rains over the last five days.

Among the affected districts were Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Vaishali, Bhagalpur and Begusarai.

"Incessant rain in various districts caused rivers and streams to overflow. Besides, heavy rainfall in catchment areas of Nepal has also led to rivers flowing above the danger level at several places," an official said, according to a report by Indian newspaper The New Indian Express.

Besides the Ganges, other rivers including Gandak, Kosi, Burhi Gandak, Punpun, Bagmati and Ghaghra are also flowing above the danger mark, officials said.

A total of 1,872 boats are currently being operated to facilitate evacuation and transportation, while around 29,400 dry ration packets and approximately 5,464 quintals of animal fodder have been distributed among flood-hit people.

Skip next section WATCH — India's repair movement takes on e-waste

WATCH — India's repair movement takes on e-waste

Replacing devices, like mobile phones, is now often easier than repairing them due to built-in obsolescence. Some Indians are fighting for the right to repair.

Skip next section Delhi police deploys 15,000 personnel ahead of BRICS Summit

Delhi police deploys 15,000 personnel ahead of BRICS Summit

Delhi police have beefed up security in the capital ahead of the annual BRICS Summit taking place this weekend. The increase consists of around 15,000 personnel and 200 companies of paramilitary forces.

The police said that the security plan had been drawn up to provide maximum security to visiting dignitaries while ensuring minimum inconvenience to the public.

"We have made elaborate bandobast [police security] by ensuring minimum inconvenience to the public. We have also issued advance advisories regarding traffic arrangements," Special Commissioner of Police Manish Kumar Agrawal said, according to a report by Indian newspaper The Hindustan Times.

Agrawal said Delhi police are working in close coordination with multiple agencies for the summit.

"Intelligence inputs will be coordinated and shared among the agencies concerned," Agrawal said.

The BRICS Summit is scheduled to be held at Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13.

Skip next section Indian government proposes legislative body for Ladakh

Indian government proposes legislative body for Ladakh

The Indian government has proposed a new Chapter K under Article 371 of the Constitution that will allow the formation of an elected body for the Union Territory (UT) of Ladakh.

The proposal came in a meeting in Delhi with a delegation of Ladakh's civil society members.

The UT-level body will have legislative power over subjects relating to environment, land, culture, language and other subject matters reserved for the UT under Article 240, civil society members said in a statement, according to a report by Indian newspaper The Hindu.

However, Ladakh's civil society members said they "are not happy" with the meeting's proceedings, as the government repeated what was discussed in the last meeting held on May 22.

"We have not got a draft of the proposal yet," Leh Apex Body (LAB) co-chairman, Chering Dorje Lakruk, who attended the latest meeting in Delhi told DW, adding that the government has promised a draft in the next meeting, which is likely to be held by the second week of October.

While expressing his disappointment over the prolonged delay, Lakruk said, "The government is buying time."

The Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), the two main political groups in Ladakh, have held several rounds of talks with the government since 2019 — when Ladakh lost its special status under Article 370 and was turned into a Union Territory, which means that unlike earlier, it is now directly governed by the Indian central government in New Delhi.

Ladakh's special status gauranteed it constitutional safeguards to preserve its unique identity, land, jobs, and environment.

Since 2019,the LAB and KDA have been demanding statehood and Sixth Schedule status for Ladakh.

Inclusion in the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution will safeguard tribal lands, local employment, and the fragile Himalayan ecology from outside conglomerates.

The groups had called for a protest march on September 10, following which the government called a meeting in Delhi on September 10.

Skip next section Welcome to our news coverage

Welcome to our news coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from DW's New Delhi bureau, bringing you the biggest headlines from India.

The Indian government has proposed the idea of forming an elected body for Kashmir's Union Territory of Ladakh, coming after years of protests and repeated demands for representation from civil society,

In Delhi, with just two days remaining before the annual BRICS Summit, commuters are already facing traffic disruptions as authorities imposed curbs on several routes.

Meanwhile, in the eastern state of Bihar, more than 4 million people remain affected by flooding.

entries.title: Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
entries.summary: Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has been on a diplomatic offensive since becoming president in April, but foreign friends may still be few and far between.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation

September 10, 2026

Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has been on a diplomatic offensive since becoming president in April, but foreign friends may still be few and far between.

Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties.

There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general's sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar's presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade.

As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He'll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven.

"Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing's transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he's really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government's allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.

"Even if they're relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw's strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar's capital.

Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low

Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself.

Since Min Aung Hlaing's military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million.

Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas.

That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere.

Despite that record, "the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections," said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia.

"The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public," Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added.

Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar

Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain.

Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc's most senior-level meetings.

Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021.

Myanmar's regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN's special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since.

Last month, the country's newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc's peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN's special envoys were no longer needed.

Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN's senior leaders summits "any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand's Thammasat University.

Marston and Marciel, though, say there's a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc's rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028.

With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country's regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same.

Thailand's premier and foreign minister "have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement," said Marston.

Japan willing to restore normal ties?

Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia's authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president.

Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was "more than ready" to restore normal relations with Myanmar.

"I don't think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country," he said.

Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so.

Will the West reengage with Myanmar?

As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them.

Pinitbhand says that's especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending.

Marston says it's possible Washington would go for "calibrated reengagement" with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010.

"But in this case, I don't think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so," he said.

Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration's list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities.

On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won't be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now.

"I don't see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy," he said. "Things could change, but that is how it looks for now."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: China: Cargo ship fire kills at least 25
entries.summary: At least five people are missing after a cargo ship caught fire at the port of Qingdao. The cause remains unclear.
entries.content:
China

China: Cargo ship fire kills at least 25

September 10, 2026

At least five people are missing after a cargo ship caught fire at the port of Qingdao. The cause remains unclear.

At least 25 people were killed and five remain missing after a fire on a cargo vessel receiving repairs at a shipyard in the northeastern Chinese port city of Qingdao, state media reported on Thursday. 

State broadcaster CCTV reported the vessel with 42 people on board caught fire at around 11:15 a.m. local time, and were extinguished around 2:30 p.m. (0630 UTC)."

The ship was identified as the 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier "Ocean Melody," which sails under a Liberian flag, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Cause remains unclear

Chinese President Xi Jinping issued has "important instructions" to conduct a search and rescue mission, while also calling for an investigation into anyone who could be responsible for the incident, Xinhua added.

Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".

It is currently unclear what could have caused the fire.

The vessel was undergoing repairs at Qingdao's Beihai Shipbuilding Co, part of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the world's largest shipbuilders.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn
